# Didache Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Hierosolymitanus (H), Didache 1

---

## Chapter 1

**1** There are two ways — one of life and one of death — and the difference between these two ways is great.

**2** The way of life is this: first, you shall love God who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And whatever you do not wish to happen to you, do not do to another.

**3** Now the teaching of these words is this: Bless those who curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for those who persecute you. For what credit is it to love those who love you? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? But as for you — love those who hate you, and you will have no enemy.

**4** Abstain from fleshly and bodily desires. If someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well, and you will be complete. If someone compels you to go one mile, go with him two. If someone takes your cloak, give him your tunic also. If someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back — for you are not even able to do so.

**5** Give to everyone who asks of you, and do not demand it back — for the Father wishes to give to all from his own gifts. Blessed is the one who gives according to the commandment, for he is blameless. Woe to the one who receives: if one who is in need receives, he is blameless; but if one who is not in need receives, he will render account as to why he received and for what purpose — and being cast into prison, he will be examined concerning what he did, and he will not be released until he has repaid the last penny.

**6** But concerning this it has also been said: Let your alms sweat in your hands until you know to whom you are giving.

---

### Council Notes

**On v.2 (The Golden Rule):** EMET and LOGOS both preserve the negative form ("do not do") which is the actual Greek phrasing. PNEUMA's "this is the rule" paraphrase sacrifices precision for accessibility. SOPHIA retains the formal structure as it mirrors Tobit 4:15 and represents the Didache's deliberate choice of the negative form over Jesus' positive form (Matt 7:12).

**On v.3 (τέλειος):** EMET renders "perfect," LOGOS "complete," PNEUMA "wholeness." SOPHIA adopts "complete" (LOGOS) as it better conveys the Greek sense of moral maturity (τέλειος) without the perfectionist connotation of "perfect" in modern English.

**On v.4 ("you are not even able to"):** All three agents preserve this frank acknowledgment of social reality — the Didache's ethic is realistic, not idealistic. The community likely had limited legal recourse.

**On v.6 (ἱδρωσάτω):** All agents agree: "sweat in your hands" must be preserved. It is a remarkable image unique to the Didache, commanding deliberate discernment in giving. The saying likely pre-dates the Didache itself.

**Ruling — "Gentiles" vs. "pagans":** EMET/LOGOS use "Gentiles" (ἔθνη), PNEUMA uses "pagans." SOPHIA retains "Gentiles" as the more accurate rendering in a Jewish-Christian context where the distinction is ethnic/covenantal as much as religious.
